transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
As President Trump campaigned in Nebraska Monday night, Vice President J.D. Vance was
in Fairbanks, Alaska, speaking at a rally for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.
They see the last frontier as their last best hope to take America in a far left direction.
Vance praised Sullivan before a crowd gathered at the Fairbanks Airport.
Sullivan is locked in a tight race with Democrat Mary Peltola for a seat expected to help determine
control of the Senate in November.
President Trump is back at the White House after campaigning for Nebraska Senator Pete
Ricketts.
Ricketts is running against Dan Osborne, an independent candidate backed by National Democrats.
During the rally, President Trump signed an executive order aimed at easing the high cost
of diesel fuel.
President Trump created a controversy over comments he made Monday night during that
campaign stop in Nebraska.
While talking about the increased gas prices because of the Iran war, he suggested that
allowing Iran to take out Los Angeles or San Diego would be a small price to pay, compared
to the war's eventual benefits.
The reaction has been quick.
Steve Futterman reports from LA.
Officials here in California are strongly criticizing the president.
Senator Gavin Newsom on social media called Trump "deranged and dangerous."
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass also had a strong response.
"You don't say things like that, you're the president of the United States."
She told NPR "irresponsible" was not a strong enough word to describe the comments.
"It's just frightening that a president of the United States would basically call on
a foreign power to attack the nation's second largest city."
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said his city is not collateral damage and is not expendable.
He told the president to keep San Diego out of his reckless war talk.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman in Los Angeles.
Now overseas, two Ethiopia pro-government forces there say they have regained control
of the country's capital, an area that has witnessed fighting in recent days from Nairobi.
Michael Kolokie reports.
The Tigray Peace Forces, a pro-government militia, says that its fighters have taken
control of the city of Mekle, the capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region.
Meanwhile, the Tigray People's Liberation Front, or TPLF, says it has retreated from
Mekle, adding that Tigray's regional government had temporarily moved out of the city and
would operate from somewhere else.
The TPLF launched a major offensive last month against the Ethiopian military, marking a
significant escalation in fighting since the country's civil war which ended four years ago.
Elsewhere, Egypt's foreign minister, Badral Abdelati, denied accusations that his country
is supporting the TPLF and its allies.
For NPR News, I'm Michael Kolokie in Nairobi.
And you're listening to NPR News.
President Trump has approved the use of a firing squad to execute the gunman, who killed
13 people and injured more than 30 others at Fort Hood, Texas in 2009.
A Pentagon spokesman said on social media Monday night that President Trump approved
the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Former Army psychiatrist Major Nidal Hassan claimed the shooting was to stop soldiers
from going to Afghanistan.
Hassan was sentenced to death in August 2013.
The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961.
Schools across the country have long struggled to hire and keep teachers for areas like special
education, math, and science.
NPR's Sanakimeta reports that most states aren't using higher pay to help fill those
jobs.
Extra pay is known to help attract and retain teachers, but the National Council on Teacher
Quality found 32 states offer no additional pay to draw and keep teachers in hard-to-fill
schools or subjects, and the study says states are actually moving away from those kinds
of incentives.
Only 13 states pay teachers extra for working in schools that have high turnover (that number
is down from 28 states in 2022), and only 17 states pay teachers more to work in hard-to-staff
subjects like math, science, or special ed (that's down from 22 states in 2022).
The report shows that high schools are struggling most at keeping teachers, especially those
serving families with low incomes.
All this comes as states face tighter budgets across the country.
Janaki Mehta, NPR News.
And I'm Giles Snyder, this is NPR News.
